articles.title: Immediate Perioperative Hypersensitivity and Anaphylaxis in Neuroanesthesia Practice: A Focused Review.
articles.abstract: Perioperative hypersensitivity reactions are uncommon but potentially catastrophic. Neurosurgical and spine patients are especially vulnerable, as the injured brain and spinal cord tolerate anaphylaxis-induced hypotension poorly, cerebral and spinal perfusion may fall precipitously, and draping of the head and torso may obscure cutaneous signs. These procedures also rely heavily on topical hemostatic agents. National audits estimate the incidence of perioperative anaphylaxis at roughly 1 in 5000 to 10,000 anesthetics, but estimates vary geographically. No study has reported a denominator-based incidence confined to neurosurgery, leaving the true burden uncharacterized for this surgical specialty. This focused review summarizes the agents, mechanisms, and perioperative implications of immediate hypersensitivity and anaphylaxis relevant to neuroanesthesia. Immediate reactions are immunologic (IgE-mediated, or IgG- and complement-mediated) or nonimmunologic (direct mast-cell activation) but converge on mast-cell and basophil mediator release, which renders their presentations largely indistinguishable. We examine agents of relevance to neurosurgery, including neuromuscular blocking agents, cefazolin and other β-lactams, chlorhexidine, sugammadex, gelatin-based and other hemostatic agents, protamine, tranexamic acid, fluorescent and dye agents, and iodinated contrast media-alongside their mechanisms and safer alternatives. Management follows international consensus recommendations centered on prompt epinephrine administration and fluid resuscitation titrated to severity. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are useful adjuncts but should not delay resuscitation. Improved outcomes depend on greater awareness, careful allergy assessment and appropriate de-labeling, surgical-anesthesia communication, and wider access to testing and dedicated surveillance.

articles.title: Incidence of venous thromboembolism with intraoperative tranexamic acid use in breast surgery patients on estrogen-containing medications: a case series.
articles.abstract: Consideration of perioperative bleeding and venous thromboembolism (VTE) are important thrombotic complications for surgeons. Tranexamic acid (TXA) is an antifibrinolytic agent that is often used perioperatively to control bleeding. Product monographs caution its use in patients using estrogen-containing medications due to theoretical increased risk of VTE. However, no studies have explored this relationship in breast surgery. This retrospective case series aimed to determine the incidence of VTE with intraoperative TXA use in breast surgery patients using estrogen-containing medication at our institution. Demographics, estrogen medications, surgical characteristics and incidence of VTE were recorded and summarized narratively. Between 2018-2025, 188 breast surgeries with intraoperative TXA administration were performed. Twelve patients used to estrogen-contain medications at the time of surgery. Eight patients used an estrogen-containing combined hormonal contraceptive. Four patients used estrogen hormone therapy. TXA was administered intravenously (N = 7) or topical irrigation (N = 5). No patients had incidence of VTE. This is the first study to describe the relationship of TXA and estrogen-containing medications in breast surgery patients. These results provide preliminary clinical data regarding a patient population for which TXA use is cautioned against. Future prospective studies are warranted to better define the risk-benefit profile of TXA in this population.

articles.title: The Impact of Tranexamic Acid Administration Route on Outcomes in Reduction Mammaplasty.
articles.abstract: Postoperative hematoma requiring unplanned intervention remains a clinically significant complication following reduction mammaplasty. Tranexamic acid (TXA) is increasingly used to reduce its occurrence and perioperative bleeding, but the optimal route of administration in breast reduction surgery remains unclear.

articles.title: A biomimetic electrospun collagen/chitosan nanofiber membrane for topical delivery of tranexamic acid.
articles.abstract: Biopolymeric nanofibers are crucial in tissue engineering, providing structural support and cell attachment. Electrospun membranes have shown potential in treating various wounds, including vascular injuries that require rapid hemostasis. In this study, a collagen (Coll)/chitosan (CTS) nanofiber membrane was fabricated via electrospinning for the topical delivery of tranexamic acid (TXA), an antifibrinolytic and first-aid agent. A key methodological innovation was the use of a non-cytotoxic PBS (1×):ethanol solvent system, ensuring biocompatibility of the final material. Collagen was extracted from bovine tendons through alkaline hydrolysis, achieving a 40% yield. FTIR spectra confirmed the presence of Type I and Type V collagen. The CTS/Coll fibers exhibited an average diameter of 127 ± 17 nm, while fibers loaded with 40 mg/ml TXA reached 375 ± 129 nm, with the drug uniformly distributed and a particle size of 105 ± 21 nm. FTIR analysis revealed electrostatic interactions between amino and hydroxyl groups of the polymers without disrupting the Coll triple helix; TXA interacted through its hydroxyl and amino groups. The TXA-loaded membrane showed a 5% increase in swelling index compared to the pure membrane. BET isotherms indicated a mesoporous structure (32.40 nm pore size), decreasing to 29.18 nm after drug incorporation. Drug release followed the Korsmeyer-Peppas model, indicating diffusion-controlled behavior. The membrane demonstrated excellent biocompatibility, timely biodegradation, and antibacterial activity. These results position the Coll/CTS nanofiber membrane as an efficient TXA delivery platform for advanced wound treatment and emergency hemorrhage control.

articles.title: A reproducible single-surgeon technique for buccal mucosa graft harvest in urethroplasty using circumferential oral retraction: technique description and case series.
articles.abstract: Buccal mucosal graft (BMG) urethroplasty is widely considered the standard technique for urethral reconstruction using a graft. Although graft placement techniques have been extensively described, less attention has been given to optimizing graft harvesting. Conventional harvesting methods typically rely on manual retraction by surgical assistants, which may limit surgical autonomy and procedural efficiency.

articles.title: Rotational Thromboelastometry (ROTEM)-Guided Assessment of Hemorrhagic Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation in Septic Shock: A Case Report of Purpura Fulminans and Multiorgan Failure.
articles.abstract: Sepsis-associated coagulopathy may progress rapidly from early thromboinflammation to overt disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) with mixed thrombotic and hemorrhagic manifestations. We report the case of a 30-year-old man with a history of methamphetamine use who presented after generalized tonic-clonic seizure activity, severe neurological impairment, hypoxemia, shock, and suspected sepsis. Initial evaluation showed severe metabolic derangement, acute kidney injury, aspiration risk during airway management, and suspected central nervous system infection. During intensive care unit evolution, the patient developed refractory septic shock, severe hypoxemic respiratory failure, rhabdomyolysis, recurrent hypoglycemia, profound mixed acidosis, anuric acute kidney injury requiring continuous renal replacement therapy, progressive thrombocytopenia, gastrointestinal bleeding, airway bleeding, catheter-site bleeding, and rapidly progressive violaceous bullous and necrotic skin lesions compatible with purpura fulminans. Clinical and laboratory findings were consistent with overt DIC with a prominent hemorrhagic phenotype. Serial rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) assessment demonstrated progressive coagulation failure, with late fibrin-based thromboelastometry (FIBTEM) findings showing severely reduced fibrin-based clot firmness consistent with fibrinogen-dependent clot failure. Hemostatic management included fibrinogen replacement, blood component therapy, tranexamic acid, and local hemostatic measures. Despite invasive mechanical ventilation, dual vasopressor therapy, corticosteroids, antimicrobial therapy, bicarbonate therapy, continuous renal replacement therapy, and targeted hemostatic resuscitation, the patient progressed to irreversible shock and cardiac arrest without return of spontaneous circulation. This case highlights the value of integrating clinical bleeding phenotype, conventional coagulation testing, DIC scoring, and viscoelastic assessment in critically ill septic patients with rapidly evolving coagulopathy.

articles.title: Safety Profile of Standardized Tranexamic Acid (TXA) Dosing in Rhytidectomy: A Retrospective Comparative Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Tranexamic acid (TXA) has been associated with reductions in intraoperative blood loss, early postoperative bleeding, time to drain removal, and postoperative ecchymosis in rhytidectomy. However, concerns regarding potential cutaneous and systemic complications persist, and interpretation of the literature is limited by variability in dosing, route of administration, and operative technique. As a result, the safety profile of TXA when mixed with local anesthetic in facelift surgery remains incompletely defined.

articles.title: Topical oxidized regenerated cellulose for perioperative blood management in total hip and knee arthroplasty: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Total hip arthroplasty (THA) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA) are established procedures for end-stage joint disease, but perioperative blood loss remains a practical concern. Oxidized regenerated cellulose (ORC) has been used as a local hemostatic material during arthroplasty; however, its comparative value in contemporary blood-management protocols remains uncertain.

articles.title: Case Report: Refractory life-threatening post-biopsy hemorrhage in a neonate successfully controlled with Ankaferd Blood Stopper.
articles.abstract: Biopsy-related hemorrhage in neonates is rare but may rapidly become life-threatening when refractory to conventional hemostatic interventions. This case is unique in reporting the first successful use of topical Ankaferd Blood Stopper® (ABS) as a salvage hemostatic agent in a neonate with infantile undifferentiated round-cell sarcoma within the differential spectrum of BCOR-altered sarcomas, an exceptionally rare malignancy, following life-threatening, refractory post-biopsy hemorrhage.

articles.title: Efficiency of Tranexamic Acid for Prevention of Bleeding In Breast Surgery: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Hematoma and seroma formation are common postoperative complications following breast surgery that adversely affect both surgical outcomes and patient recovery. Tranexamic acid (TXA) is increasingly recognized as an effective prophylactic agent; however, evidence regarding its efficacy in breast surgery remains limited.
